strengths: Novel framing that focuses on the visual encoder as a source of hallucination, complementing the more common LLM-decoding-side literature (VCD, OPERA).

Fairly comprehensive empirical evaluation across three LVLM families (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP, Qwen-VL) and multiple benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE on three datasets, MME hallucination subset and full set, GPT4o-aided LLaVA-Bench), with consistent gains over vanilla and prior training-free baselines in most settings.
Extensive ablations (module-wise ablation, alpha/beta/K/l sweeps) and qualitative visualizations/case studies that make the mechanism of each component reasonably interpretable.

The three proposed mechanisms (token re-weighting, token subtraction via noise, adversarial-attack contrastive decoding) are individually simple and map cleanly onto the three diagnosed problems (statistical bias, inherent bias, vulnerability), which aids clarity of exposition.
weaknesses: The claim of being 'the first to trace LVLM hallucinations to visual encoders' is overstated; the paper itself cites prior work on CLIP token overemphasis/attention sinks [9,14], adversarial fragility of CLIP-like encoders [25], and long-tail/imbalanced pretraining concept bias [27] — these already implicate the visual encoder, so the core diagnostic claims are largely a repackaging/extension of known phenomena rather than a new discovery.

The statistical-bias analysis (Fig. 2a) and inherent-bias analysis (Fig. 2b) are purely correlational (based on one model, LLaVA-1.5) and do not establish a causal link between encoder-level norm overemphasis/noise-response and downstream hallucination; no controlled intervention (e.g., directly suppressing high-norm tokens with a real query image and measuring effect independent of the proposed method) is shown to validate the diagnosis in isolation.

Token re-weighting relies on a caption generated by the same 'vanilla' LVLM whose hallucinations the method is trying to fix; the paper's justification that hallucinated objects 'fail to match any visual tokens with high similarity' is asserted without empirical verification (e.g., no ablation quantifying re-weighting robustness under captions with varying hallucination rates).

The 'training-free' framing is somewhat misleading in terms of computational cost: the method requires (a) an extra forward pass through the vanilla LVLM to get a caption, (b) K forward passes through the encoder for noise tokens (though pre-computable), and (c) a per-image gradient-based adversarial optimization loop through the encoder/text-encoder — this is test-time optimization, and Table 11 shows ~7.6x inference overhead versus vanilla, comparable to OPERA, undermining the 'efficient alternative' positioning claimed in the introduction relative to training-based methods.

Results are mixed for InstructBLIP: gains are consistently smaller and sometimes negligible or negative (e.g., Table 4 Count score 75.3 vs 75.0, POPE Random split where OPERA outperforms SHIELD), and the paper's explanation (Q-Former constraining visual feature usage) is not further investigated or mitigated, leaving open whether the method is broadly architecture-agnostic as claimed.

Baseline comparison is limited to two training-free methods (VCD, OPERA); no comparison to more recent or additional training-free/training-based hallucination-mitigation baselines, and no statistical significance testing (e.g., variance across seeds/samples) is reported despite modest sample sizes (500 images for CHAIR).

The method introduces four sensitive hyperparameters (alpha, beta, K, l) tuned via ablation on a single benchmark/model (LLaVA-1.5 CHAIR); it is unclear whether the same fixed values generalize well across the very different architectures tested, given the noted weaker performance on InstructBLIP.

GPT4o-aided evaluation, while informative, is a single-judge, LLM-based metric susceptible to known biases (verbosity, position, self-preference) and the paper does not perform any human-agreement validation of GPT4o's scoring.

strengths: The paper offers a relatively novel framing by attributing LVLM hallucinations to the visual encoder rather than the LLM decoder, which is an underexplored angle relative to most prior training-free hallucination mitigation work.

The proposed taxonomy of statistical bias, inherent bias, and vulnerability is intuitive and each is paired with a targeted, lightweight intervention (token re-weighting, token subtraction, adversarial contrastive decoding).

Experiments span multiple LVLM backbones (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP, Qwen-VL) and multiple benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE with 3 datasets, MME hallucination subset and full set, GPT4o-aided evaluation on LLaVA-Bench), giving reasonably broad empirical coverage.

Ablation studies (module ablation, hyperparameter sweeps for alpha, beta, K, l) and qualitative visualizations/case studies help substantiate that each proposed component contributes incrementally to the overall gains.
The method is training-free and largely model-agnostic, which is practically appealing compared to RLHF/fine-tuning-based approaches.
weaknesses: The causal claims linking the three 'issues' to hallucination are largely correlational (e.g., Figure 2a shows a correlation between peak-to-average L2 ratio and hallucination rate, not causation), and the taxonomy's three categories (statistical bias vs. inherent bias) overlap substantially in mechanism, both stemming from imbalanced pretraining data, making the framing feel somewhat post-hoc relative to the three independently designed technical modules.

Token re-weighting relies on a 'naive caption' generated by the same (potentially hallucinating) vanilla LVLM to re-weight visual tokens; the justification that hallucinated objects 'fail to match any visual tokens with high similarity' is asserted rather than rigorously tested/verified, leaving a partially circular design underexamined.

The efficiency claim implicit in being 'training-free' is significantly undermined by the reported inference overhead: SHIELD is 7.6x slower than vanilla decoding (Table 11), only modestly better than OPERA (12.4x), due to per-sample naive caption generation, multiple noise-based encoder passes, and gradient-based adversarial attack optimization at inference time — this is a serious practical drawback not adequately discussed as a limitation in the main text.

The adversarial attack + contrastive decoding module is conceptually similar to existing distortion-based contrastive decoding (e.g., VCD), and the paper does not clearly differentiate why a learned per-image adversarial perturbation is fundamentally superior to VCD's simpler blur/noise-based contrast, beyond empirical gains; the added complexity/cost is not well motivated against this simpler baseline.

Empirical results are mixed in places: InstructBLIP POPE improvements are limited (explicitly attributed to Q-Former constraints, weakening the generality claim), OPERA sometimes wins on individual attribute scores (e.g., color/position in MME Table 4, several MME cognition subtasks in Table 10), and K=64 in the ablation shows the method degrading rather than saturating, suggesting some fragility of hyperparameters.

Comparisons are limited to only two training-free baselines (VCD, OPERA); several more recent training-free decoding methods for LVLM hallucination mitigation are not included, making it hard to assess how competitive SHIELD is against the current state of the art.

Evaluation scale is modest (500 images for CHAIR, presumably small LLaVA-Bench set for GPT4o evaluation) with no reported variance/multiple runs, and GPT4o-based evaluation is used as a primary metric for correctness/detailedness despite known biases and lack of human validation of GPT4o's judgments.

The four hyperparameters (alpha, beta, K, l) require tuning and are reported as fixed across three different LVLM families, but the sensitivity analysis (Appendix C) is only conducted on one model (LLaVA-1.5), leaving open whether the chosen values generalize well or were implicitly tuned to that model.

strengths: Novel and clearly motivated framing that traces LVLM hallucinations to the visual encoder rather than the LLM, complementing (not just duplicating) the dominant line of work that focuses on LLM-side decoding fixes.

The three identified failure modes (statistical bias, inherent bias, vulnerability) are each supported by a small empirical analysis (Fig. 2) before the method is introduced, giving the design some grounding rather than being purely ad hoc.

Each of the three proposed components maps cleanly onto one diagnosed problem, and the module ablation (Table 6) shows each piece contributes incremental gains, which is a good sanity check on the paper's causal story.

Broad evaluation across three LVLM families (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP, Qwen-VL) and multiple hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE on three datasets, MME hallucination subset, GPT4o-assisted LLaVA-Bench evaluation), with mostly consistent improvements over VCD and OPERA.
Reasonably thorough hyperparameter ablations (alpha, beta, K, l) and inference-overhead reporting, which aids reproducibility and practical assessment of the trade-offs.

Honest reporting of some limitations/negative results (e.g., InstructBLIP's Q-Former reducing benefits, weaker performance on knowledge-heavy MME cognition subtasks), which increases the credibility of the claims.
weaknesses: The 'vulnerability' component is conceptually very close to VCD's core mechanism (contrasting clean vs. perturbed image outputs); the main difference is that the perturbation is now adversarially optimized rather than blurred/noised. This narrows the actual novelty gap versus the closest baseline more than the framing suggests.

The method has real cost: it requires generating a naive caption with the vanilla LVLM, running a CLIP text encoder, and performing an online gradient-based adversarial attack at inference time, resulting in ~7.6x inference latency versus vanilla (Table 11) — a substantial overhead that is understated relative to the 'training-free' framing (training-free does not mean inference-cheap).

The token re-weighting step depends on a naive caption generated by the same (hallucination-prone) vanilla LVLM; the paper's justification that hallucinated objects 'fail to match any visual tokens' is asserted rather than empirically verified (e.g., no ablation replacing the naive caption with a stronger/oracle caption to isolate its effect).

Results are mixed in several places that weaken the 'broad applicability' claim: InstructBLIP underperforms OPERA on POPE COCO average and Count subset of MME (Table 4), and SHIELD underperforms vanilla/OPERA/VCD on MME cognition tasks requiring prior/world knowledge (Numerical Calculation, Text Translation, Code Reasoning, Table 10), suggesting the contrastive decoding may suppress useful LLM priors, not just hallucinations.

No variance/error bars or multiple-run statistics are reported for any benchmark, making it hard to judge whether the reported gains (some of which are only 1-2 points) are statistically meaningful, especially given the relatively small CHAIR sample (500 images) and small-scale MME subsets.

Comparisons are limited to VCD and OPERA (both from 2024); no comparison to other recent training-free or lightweight training-required hallucination-mitigation baselines is included, leaving the relative standing of SHIELD against the broader current landscape unclear.

The method assumes a CLIP-style vision encoder with a paired text encoder, which is used for both the naive-caption similarity re-weighting and the adversarial attack loss; applicability to non-CLIP visual encoders (e.g., SigLIP, DINO-based encoders increasingly used in LVLMs) is not discussed or evaluated.

strengths: Identifies a relatively underexplored source of LVLM hallucination (the visual encoder) rather than the more commonly studied LLM decoding stage, and supports this diagnosis with targeted empirical analyses (Fig. 2) correlating token overemphasis, dominant-object bias under noise input, and adversarial vulnerability with hallucination rates.

Proposes a training-free framework (SHIELD) with three complementary, individually interpretable modules (token re-weighting, token subtraction, adversarial contrastive decoding) each mapped to a specific diagnosed issue.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: CHAIR, POPE (multiple datasets/splits), MME (hallucination subset and full set), AMBER, GPT-4o-assisted evaluation on LLaVA-Bench, and MMHal-Bench, across three LVLM backbones (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP, Qwen-VL), plus appendix extensions to Qwen2/2.5/3-VL showing some generalization to newer models.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (module-wise contribution, hyperparameters α/β/K/l, attack-step count, attack strategy vs. FGSM/PGD, plausible-hallucination robustness of naive captions) and an efficiency/overhead analysis comparing runtime and memory against baselines.

Comparison against a wide set of both training-free and training-required baselines (Table 16) shows the method is competitive even against methods that require additional fine-tuning, which strengthens the practical significance of a training-free approach.
Case studies and visualizations (attention maps, hallucination histograms, robustness curves) provide qualitative support for the claimed mechanisms.
weaknesses: The claim of being 'first to trace hallucinations to visual encoders' is somewhat overstated; prior works cited by the authors themselves (Darcet et al. 2024 on ViT registers/attention artifacts, Kang et al. 2025 on visual attention sinks, Parashar et al. 2024 on long-tailed pretraining concepts) already document closely related phenomena, so the novelty largely lies in packaging these into a hallucination-mitigation pipeline rather than a fundamentally new diagnosis.

The token re-weighting module depends on a naive caption generated by the same (potentially hallucinating) vanilla LVLM; the paper's argument that hallucinated objects 'fail to match any visual tokens with high similarity' is asserted rather than rigorously proven, and while an appendix ablation shows limited performance drop, this is only tested in one controlled setting.

The overall method has many interacting heuristic components and hyperparameters (α, β, K, l, attack steps, caption length), raising concerns about robustness/generalization and the effort required to tune it for new models or domains beyond what is shown.

Non-trivial computational overhead (~3x inference time and increased memory vs. vanilla decoding, driven mainly by caption generation and adversarial tensor optimization), which somewhat undercuts the practicality advantage typically claimed for training-free methods, especially for real-time applications mentioned in the introduction (autonomous systems, robotics).

Results are inconsistent for InstructBLIP (Table 3, weaker/occasionally worse than OPERA) and for several MME cognition subtasks (numerical calculation, text translation, code reasoning all regress vs. vanilla/VCD in Table 13), which tempers the 'broad applicability' claim.

GPT-4o-assisted evaluation compares all four systems' outputs to the judge simultaneously in one prompt (Table 10), which can introduce relative-comparison biases; no inter-rater reliability or repeated-trial variance is reported for this or other stochastic (sampling-based decoding) experiments.

In the extended comparison (Table 16), some training-based baselines (e.g., MCA-LLaVA) achieve comparable or better CI than SHIELD, so the improvement over the strongest existing methods is more modest than the headline framing suggests.

strengths: Extensive empirical validation across multiple LVLM families (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP, Qwen-VL, and even newer Qwen2/2.5/3-VL variants in the appendix) and multiple hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MME, AMBER, LLaVA-Bench with GPT-4o judge, MMHal-Bench).
Thorough ablation studies on each module and on all hyperparameters (alpha, beta, K, learning rate, attack steps), plus an inference-overhead/efficiency analysis.
The method is training-free and can be applied at inference time without modifying model weights, which is practically appealing.
Reasonably clear visualizations (attention maps, radar charts, hallucination histograms) and case studies that illustrate the intended effect of each module.
weaknesses: The central novelty claim ('first to trace LVLM hallucinations to visual encoders') is overstated; prior work on attention sinks/register tokens (Darcet et al. 2024), visual over-trust (OPERA), and visual-contrastive decoding (VCD) already implicate encoder-level artifacts in hallucination, so the positioning against related work is not fully convincing.

The three proposed fixes are fairly ad hoc engineering interventions (similarity-based re-weighting, noise-averaged subtraction, adversarially-crafted perturbation + contrastive decoding) without strong theoretical justification for why they correctly isolate 'statistical bias', 'inherent bias', and 'vulnerability' as cleanly separable phenomena versus confounded effects.

The pipeline has a circular dependency: a naive caption is generated by the same (hallucination-prone) vanilla LVLM and then used to correct hallucinations; the robustness argument in Appendix D.2 is based on a single qualitative example and a small quantitative check, which is not sufficiently rigorous.

Significant inference overhead (~3x runtime and increased memory vs. vanilla model, Table 8/9) mostly from caption generation and adversarial optimization, which undercuts the practical 'training-free/efficient' selling point, especially for real-time use cases mentioned in future work.

Method requires white-box access to the visual encoder, a paired CLIP text encoder, and the ability to backprop through the vision tower to craft adversarial perturbations and compute re-weighting/subtraction — this limits applicability to only models with exposed CLIP-style visual encoders and undermines generality claims across 'diverse LVLM families.'

Mixed/inconsistent results undercut the strength of claims: SHIELD underperforms OPERA on InstructBLIP POPE-Random (88.2 vs 89.8) and on some MME cognition subtasks (e.g., Numerical Calculation, Text Translation), and the paper's post-hoc explanations (e.g., Q-Former constraints) feel speculative rather than substantiated.

The GPT-4o-assisted evaluation and the AMBER/MMHal comparisons use the method's own favorable hyperparameters tuned on CHAIR/LLaVA-1.5, with no clear discussion of whether hyperparameters were re-tuned per benchmark/model, raising concerns about selective reporting.

The diagnostic experiments motivating the three issues (Figure 2) are conducted only on LLaVA-1.5/POPE-COCO, yet are used to justify a general theory of hallucination causation across all LVLMs; broader validation of the underlying diagnosis itself (not just the fix) is limited.

strengths: Novel framing that shifts the locus of hallucination analysis from the LLM decoder to the visual encoder, identifying three distinct failure modes (statistical bias, inherent bias, vulnerability) supported by preliminary empirical analysis (Fig. 2).

Very extensive experimental validation: CHAIR, POPE (across COCO/A-OKVQA/GQA, 3 splits), MME (hallucination subset and full set), AMBER, GPT-4o-assisted evaluation on LLaVA-Bench, and MMHal-Bench, across three different LVLM backbones (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP, Qwen-VL), plus additional tests on newer Qwen2/2.5/3-VL variants.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each module (token re-weighting, token subtraction, contrastive decoding) and sensitivity analyses over all key hyperparameters (α, β, K, l, attack steps).

Comparison against a wide range of both training-free and training-based baselines (DoLa, ICD, VCD, TAME, OPERA, SID, LLaVA-RLHF, CCA-LLaVA, MCA-LLaVA), showing SHIELD is competitive or superior while remaining training-free.
Reasonable efficiency/overhead analysis breaking down the computational cost contributed by each module, and acknowledgment of limitations for real-time use.

Supplementary analyses addressing likely concerns (e.g., impact of hallucinated naive captions, comparison of learnable attack vs. fixed-step adversarial attacks, class-wise inherent bias breakdown) suggest a well-considered and carefully revised submission.
weaknesses: The claim of being 'the first to trace LVLM hallucinations to visual encoders' is strong and somewhat overstated given that prior training-free methods (e.g., VCD, which perturbs the input image) already implicitly probe visual-encoder robustness; the novelty framing could be more precisely scoped.

The method pipeline depends on generating a naive caption with the vanilla (potentially hallucinating) LVLM for token re-weighting, which introduces a circularity risk; the robustness analysis in the appendix is based on a single qualitative example and a small-scale quantitative check, which is not fully convincing.

Token subtraction for 'inherent bias' uses a single global average over K noise-derived embeddings subtracted uniformly from all visual tokens, which is a fairly coarse correction without strong theoretical justification for why this generalizes across diverse images/objects.

Computational overhead is non-trivial (~2.8x runtime increase over vanilla decoding, plus extra memory), driven mainly by caption generation and per-sample adversarial tensor optimization, which limits practicality for real-time or large-scale deployment despite being 'training-free.'

Mixed results in some settings (e.g., InstructBLIP shows limited gains, and OPERA outperforms SHIELD in certain POPE random/popular splits on InstructBLIP), with explanations (Q-Former constraints) that are plausible but not empirically verified in depth.
No variance/statistical-significance reporting across multiple runs or seeds, making it hard to assess the robustness of reported improvements, especially the smaller margins in some benchmarks.
All experiments are confined to 7B/8B-scale models; no results at larger model scales are provided to confirm the method's generalization to bigger LVLMs.

The adversarial-attack-based vulnerability module requires access to a paired CLIP-style text encoder for constructing the attack tensor, which may limit applicability to LVLMs whose visual encoders are not CLIP-derived or lack a paired text encoder.
